Makes it possible for you to specify options for printing files or the contents of the Command window or Clipboard.

This dialog box appears when you select Options in the Print dialog box. For more information, see Print Dialog Box ([[T0]]).

Specifies the type and the file to print.
 **Type**
Specifies the type of file to print. Caution The [[T0]] File option bypasses the printer driver and sends the contents of the selected file directly to the printer. Make sure that the file contains valid printer commands. Sending invalid printer commands to the printer device might cause the printer to fail and require a reset.
**File**
Specifies the path and file name of the file you want to print. To browse for and select a file, click the ellipsis (...) button to open the Print File dialog box. For more information, see Print File Dialog Box .

Specifies output options for the file.
 **Line numbers**
Prints line numbers in the left margin. This option is available for printing contents of the Command window and the Clipboard.
**Page eject before**
Advances the printer to the top of the next page before printing the file.
**Page eject after**
Advances the printer to the top of the next page after printing the file. This option is not available for reports and labels.
**Restore environment**
When running [[T0]] version 2. x reports, makes sure that the data environment settings previously saved with the report are used to run the report. This option does not apply to [[T1]] reports because they use their own data environments.
**Options**
Displays the Report and Label Print Options dialog box for selecting records you wan to print from a report or label. Available only when printing reports and labels. For more information, see Report and Label Print Options Dialog Box .

[[T0]] makes it possible for you to share a connection handle for a remote data connection. Sharing a connection handle can be desirable when you want to manage [[T1]] Server connections and server resources better by reducing the number of connections.

By default, [[T2]] creates a new connection handle each time a remote data connection is created. However, when specified, [[T3]] can use an existing connection and associate the new statement with it. This creates a new statement handle and [[T4]] handle; however, the associated connection handle is the same.

There are three types of handles associated with a remote data connection. The following table describes these handles.

| Handle type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Connection handle ([[T5]]) | A unique integer assigned to a connection. |
| Statement handle ([[T6]]) | A unique integer assigned to a statement. Note More than one [[T7]] statement handle can be associated with a [[T8]] connection handle. |
| [[T9]] connection handle | A unique integer assigned by [[T10]] to a unique statement handle. |

A remote view can use a shared connection handle by including the [[T0]] keyword in the [[T1]] command. If a shared connection is available, [[T2]] uses it to create a new statement handle and [[T3]] connection handle. If a shared connection is unavailable, [[T4]] creates a new, shared connection that other views can use.

You can create a new connection that can be shared by including the [[T0]] parameter in the [[T1]] command. The [[T2]] command always creates a new connection, statement, and [[T3]] connection handle.

Including the [[T4]] parameter in the [[T5]] command also creates a new connection that can be shared; however, including the [[T6]] parameter causes [[T7]] to use a currently shared connection and creates only a new statement handle and [[T8]] connection handle.

textos.c94d4b30-e6aa-408c-a29d-6b27eb93674d#148:
If you want to protect data during updates, use buffers. [[T0]] record and table buffering help you protect data update and data maintenance operations on single records and on multiple records of data in multiuser environments. Buffers can automatically test, lock, and release records or tables.

With buffering, you can easily detect and resolve conflicts in data update operations: the current record is copied to a memory or disk location managed by [[T1]]. Other users can then still access the original record simultaneously. When you move from the record or try to update the record programmatically, [[T2]] attempts to lock the record, verify that no other changes have been made by other users, and then write the changes. After you attempt to update data, you must also resolve conflicts that prevent the changes from being written to the original table.

Before you enable buffering, evaluate the data environment to choose the buffering method and locking options that best suit the editing needs of your application, the record and table types and sizes, how the information is used and updated, and other factors. Once you enable buffering, it remains in effect until you disable buffering or close the table.

[[T0]] has two types of buffering: record and table.
 - To access, modify, and write a single record at a time, choose record buffering. Record buffering provides appropriate process validation with minimal impact on the data update operations of other users in a multiuser environment.
- To buffer the updates to several records, choose table buffering. Table buffering provides the most effective way to handle several records in one table or child records in a one-to-many relationship.
- To provide maximum protection for existing data, use [[T1]] transactions. You can use transactions alone, but you gain additional effectiveness by using transactions as wrappers for record or table buffering commands.
[[T0]] provides buffering in two locking modes: pessimistic and optimistic. These choices determine when one or more records are locked, and how and when they're released.

Pessimistic buffering prevents other users in a multiuser environment from accessing a particular record or table while you're making changes to it. A pessimistic lock provides the most secure environment for changing individual records but it can slow user operations. This buffering mode is most similar to the standard locking mechanism in previous versions of [[T0]], with the added benefit of built-in data buffering.

Optimistic buffering is an efficient way to update records because locks are only taken at the time the record is written, thus minimizing the time any single user monopolizes the system in a multiuser environment. When you use record or table buffering on views, [[T0]] imposes optimistic locking.

The value of the Buffering property, set with the [[T1]] Function function, determines the buffering and locking methods.

The following table summarizes valid values for the Buffering property.

| To enable | Use this value |
| --- | --- |
| No buffering. The default value. | 1 |
| Pessimistic record locks which lock record now, update when pointer moves or upon [[T2]] . | 2 |
| Optimistic record locks which wait until pointer moves, and then lock and update. | 3 |
| Pessimistic table locks which lock record now, update later upon [[T3]]. | 4 |
| Optimistic table lock which wait until [[T4]], and then lock and update edited records. | 5 |

The default value for Buffering is 1 for tables and 3 for views. If you use buffering to access remote data, the Buffering property is either 3, optimistic row buffering, or 5, optimistic table buffering. For more information on accessing data in remote tables, see How to: Query Multiple Tables and Views.

> **Note:** Set [[T5]] to [[T6]] for all buffering modes above 1.

Most fonts can be displayed in a wide variety of sizes, and some are proportionally spaced. A row corresponds to the height of the current font; a column corresponds to the average width of a letter in the current font.

In [[T0]] for Windows and [[T1]] for Macintosh, you can position the text-editing region in a window with decimal fractions for row and column coordinates. In [[T2]] for [[T3]]-[[T4]], decimal fractions used for row and column coordinates are rounded to the nearest integer value.

 [[T5]] [[T6]], [[T7]] [, [[T8]]]

 The [[T9]] clause must be included to specify the height and width of the text-editing region. The height of the text-editing region in rows is specified by [[T10]], and the width in columns is specified by [[T11]].

 If [[T12]] is 1, a special one-line text-editing region is created. You can scroll horizontally in the one-line region. Pressing Enter moves you to the next object.

 The optional numeric expression [[T13]] specifies the number of characters in the memory variable, array element or field that can be edited, starting with the first character. If [[T14]] is omitted, all of the memory variable, array element or field can be edited.

 In [[T15]] for Windows and [[T16]] for Macintosh, the text-editing region font determines the size of the editing region. The text-editing region font is specified with the [[T17]] clause. If the [[T18]] clause is omitted, the text-editing region uses the font of its parent window (the main [[T19]] window or a user-defined window).

 [[T20]] [[T21]]

You can include the I or J options in the [[T0]] clause to specify how text is justified in the text-editing region, and the 2 or 3 options to specify the appearance of the text-editing region. The 2 (two-dimensional) and 3 (three-dimensional) options are only available in [[T1]] for Macintosh. Any additional characters included in the [[T2]] clause are ignored.

 Option Purpose

 ------ -------

 I Centers text in the text-editing region.

 J Right-justifies text. Text in the text-editing region is left-justified by default.

 2 Creates a flat (two-dimensional) text-editing region. This is the default text-editing region in [[T3]] for Macintosh.

 3 Creates a three-dimensional text-editing region identical to text-editing regions in [[T4]] for Macintosh.

 This example creates a text-editing region in which text is right-justified:

 [[T5]] 'This will be edited' [[T6]] text

 @ 2,2 [[T7]] text [[T8]] 'J' [[T9]] 5, 50

 [[T10]]

 This example creates a three-dimensional text-editing region in [[T11]] for Macintosh:

 [[T12]] 'This will be edited' [[T13]] text

 @ 2,2 [[T14]] text [[T15]] '3' [[T16]] 5, 50

 [[T17]] [[T18]][, [[T19]]]

 The character expression [[T20]] is the name of the font, and the numeric expression [[T21]] is the font size. For example, the following clause can be used to display the text in the text-editing region in 16-point Courier font:

 [[T22]] 'Courier', 16

If you include the [[T0]] clause but omit the font size [[T1]], a 10-point font is used.

 If the [[T2]] clause is omitted and the text-editing region is placed in the main [[T3]] window, the main [[T4]] window font is used. If the [[T5]] clause is omitted and the text-editing region is placed in a user-defined window, the user-defined window font is used.

 If the font you specify is not available, a font with similar font characteristics is substituted.

 The [[T6]] clause is ignored in [[T7]] for [[T8]]-[[T9]].

 [[T10]] [[T11]]

 In [[T12]] for Windows and [[T13]] for Macintosh, include the [[T14]] clause to specify a font style for the text-editing region. If the font style you specify is not available, a font style with similar characteristics is substituted.

 The font style is specified with [[T15]]. If the [[T16]] clause is omitted, the standard font style is used.

 Character Font Style

 --------- ----------

 B Bold

 C Condense*

 E Extend*

 I Italic

 N Normal

 O Outline

 Q Opaque

 S Shadow

 - Strikeout*

 T Transparent

 U Underline

 * The Condense and Extend styles are only available in [[T17]] for Macintosh. The Strikeout style is only available in [[T18]] for Windows.

 You can include more than one character to specify a combination of font styles. For example, the following clause specifies Bold Italic:

 [[T19]] '[[T20]]'

 The [[T21]] clause is ignored in [[T22]] for [[T23]]-[[T24]].

[[T0]] expr

 When you edit the text in a text-editing region, the text is read from and saved to the memory variable, array element or field specified with memvar or field. If you specify a memory variable that doesn't exist, it is automatically created and initialized if you include the [[T1]] clause. However, an array element isn't created if you specify an array element in a [[T2]] clause. The [[T3]] clause is ignored if the memory variable already exists or you specify a table or memo field.

 -------------------------------

 Note - If the [[T4]] clause isn't included and memvar doesn't exist, the error message "Variable not found" appears.

 -------------------------------

 The [[T5]] expression expr determines the type of memory variable created and its initial value. It must be of character or memo type. Here are examples of [[T6]] clauses for text-editing regions:

 @ 2,2 [[T7]] text [[T8]] 'This will be edited' [[T9]] 5, 50

 [[T10]]

 @ 2,2 [[T11]] text [[T12]](20) [[T13]] 5, 50

 [[T14]] | [[T15]]

 Text-editing regions are by default enabled when [[T16]] or [[T17]] is issued. Include [[T18]] to prevent a text-editing region from being selected when [[T19]] or [[T20]] is issued. A disabled text-editing region cannot be selected and appears in disabled colors. Use [[T21]] to enable a disabled text-editing region.
